metadata.title: Skills and labour market performance in Sweden

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) 2012 microdata for Sweden to estimate literacy proficiency distributions and run multivariate OLS and logit regressions. It reports regression coefficients and odds ratios but does not document the use of PIAAC sampling weights or replicate-weight variance estimation in the provided text. Because the analysis is based on survey data with complex sampling, analysts should apply the appropriate PIAAC student/household sampling weights when producing population-representative estimates and use the corresponding replicate weights (if available) for correct standard errors. The manuscript’s tables do not specify a weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT), so the weighting approach cannot be verified from the excerpt.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the reported models are literacy score points and employment/training participation outcomes derived from PIAAC, but the excerpt does not describe whether literacy scores are treated as PV-based achievement estimates or as scaled scores (e.g., WLE/theta). The paper also does not report any explicit missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation) for the regression samples. This is therefore a reporting gap: the methodology section would need to specify how missing responses and the construction of literacy scores were handled to assess robustness and comparability.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The literacy-score OLS regression (Table 1) excludes students in full-time education (any age) and excludes young people both in education and employment and aged under 25; the reference category is a man aged 35–44 living in Eastern Sweden with upper secondary education and at least one parent with upper secondary education. The employment logit regressions (Tables 2, 5) similarly exclude students in full-time education (any age) and youth both in education and employment and aged under 25, and note that individuals inactive represent around 17% of the whole sample. The adult education/training logit regression (Table 3) excludes students in full-time education (any age) and youth both in education and employment and aged under 25. For immigrant-only regressions (Tables 4 and 5), the sample is restricted to foreign-born and foreign-speaker adults, with Table 4 noting 515 observations for the first two regressions and 447 for the third due to missing occupational category.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) 2012 for Sweden to describe adult literacy proficiency and to estimate how literacy and socio-demographic factors relate to employment and participation in adult education and training. The analysis reports multivariate OLS regressions for literacy determinants (R² = 0.39; n = 3687 after exclusions) and logit regressions for employment and AET participation. Across specifications, literacy is strongly associated with labour market outcomes: a one-standard-deviation increase in literacy corresponds to 85% higher odds of being employed (and 30% higher odds of participating in adult education/training). For immigrants, literacy and time since immigration are key predictors of literacy and employment, with employment gaps largely explained by lower literacy proficiency. Limitations include the absence of explicit documentation of plausible-value handling and missing-data strategy in the provided text, and the caution that reverse causality may exist between skills and employment.
